column8: In March 1815 Napoleon escaped from exile on Elba and took back the throne of France. The powers of Europe declared war on him. Two of their armies were already in Belgium: the Duke of Wellington's army of British, Dutch, Belgian and German troops around Brussels, and Field Marshal Bloocher's Prussian army around Nah-moor. Napoleon decided to strike before the rest could join them.

Before dawn on 15 June the French army, about 120,000 men, crossed the river Sahm-bruh at Shar-luh-rwah. Napoleon aimed his blow at the point where the two allied armies met, to drive between them and beat each one alone. The Prussian outposts fell back fighting toward Fluh-roos.

That evening the officers of Wellington's army were at a ball in Brussels. During it, news came that the French were not where Wellington had expected. According to a witness, he said that Napoleon had humbugged him, and had gained twenty-four hours' march on him. Officers left the ballroom in their dancing shoes to join their regiments.

On the 16th Napoleon attacked Bloocher's Prussians, about eighty thousand men, around the villages of Leenyee and San Tah-mahn. All afternoon the two armies fought for the villages, house by house. In the evening Napoleon sent in the Imperial Guard, and the Prussian centre broke.

At the same time, eleven kilometres away, Marshal Nay attacked the crossroads of Kat-ruh Brah, held at first only by Dutch and Belgian troops under the Prince of Orange. Wellington arrived, and all afternoon his regiments came up the road from Brussels and were thrown into the fight. By nightfall Nay had been held, and the crossroads was still in allied hands.

Between the two battles, a whole French corps, twenty thousand men under dairlon, marched back and forth on conflicting orders, and fought at neither. With it, Napoleon might have destroyed the Prussians at Leenyee, or Nay might have taken Kat-ruh Brah.

At Leenyee, the seventy-two-year-old Bloocher led a last cavalry charge. His horse was shot and fell on him, and French cuirassiers rode over him in the dusk. An aide hid him and got him away. While he was missing, his chief of staff, Gny-zuh-now, ordered the beaten army to retreat north, to Wahvruh.

Retreating north to Wahvruh, not east toward their homeland, kept the Prussians close enough to help Wellington. It was the decision that made Waterloo possible. Napoleon, thinking them beaten, sent Marshal Grooshee with about thirty thousand men to follow them, and Grooshee went first toward Zhahm-bloo.

Learning that the Prussians had fallen back, Wellington withdrew from Kat-ruh Brah along the Brussels road to a ridge he had chosen near the village of Mon San Zhon. In the afternoon a violent thunderstorm broke over the armies. The French followed through the mud, and the British cavalry fought a rearguard action at Zhuh-nap.

All night the rain fell on two armies lying in the open fields, a few kilometres apart. Wellington would stand and fight on the ridge, because Bloocher had promised to come to him from Wahvruh. At dawn, the first Prussian corps set off along muddy lanes toward the sound of the guns that had not yet begun.

In the morning Napoleon waited for the ground to dry so that his guns could move. At Wahl-an, Grooshee heard the first cannon to the west, and kept marching after the Prussians as he had been ordered. The battle of Waterloo was about to begin.
